name: Sean-nós dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: An old-timer from the Connemara Gaeltacht with effortless rhythm
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Sean-nós dance represents an older, informal style of solo Irish dancing documented by historians and ethnomusicologists.
The term 'sean-nós' was formally applied to the dance form in 1976, distinguishing it from newer competitive stepdance forms.
on_screen: Map: Ireland · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed informally at pub sessions, folk festivals, and community gatherings, as well as specialized events and competitions like Oireachtas na Samhna and Comórtas Damhsa Chóilín Sheáin Dharach.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features low-to-the-ground footwork, improvised steps, and a percussive batter that emphasizes the musical beat.
Dancers perform solo or take turns in small groups without physical contact, keeping arms loose and natural.
Watch for batter.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (zcYMvXDKLlY)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: solo or small groups dancing in turns without physical contact

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Accompaniment is provided by a lively traditional Irish band, featuring instruments like the fiddle and accordion.
Standard traditional tunes such as McCleod's reel and New Mown Meadows frequently accompany the performance.
Listen for the fiddle, accordion.
Lively traditional Irish band music featuring fiddle and accordion accompaniment that matches the percussive battering of the dancer's feet.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear casual everyday clothing without standardized costuming.
Traditionally, performances take place on tight wooden surfaces such as a door taken off its hinges, a table, a barrel, or a stool.
on_screen: Image gallery: 6 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Figures such as Johnny Connolly, Maldon Meehan, and Ronan Regan are noted in connection with the living tradition and preservation of sean-nós dancing.
The dance features regional stylistic subtypes, notably separated into Connemara-style and Munster-style traditions within the western Irish Gaeltacht.
Sean-nós dance is considered the historical predecessor that influenced modern competitive Irish stepdance as well as forms like North American tap dance.
